The method constructs minimally unsatisfiable clause sets from selected first-order literals, then forms theorems by retaining some clauses as premises and taking the negation of one clause, or a conjunction of clauses, as the conclusion. Minimal unsatisfiability ensures that the remaining premises are satisfiable, avoiding trivial inference by explosion, while unsatisfiability of the full set guarantees the resulting entailment. Theorems are therefore correct by construction, without a separate proof procedure for each instance. Extending the previously developed $\Delta_1$ generator, we introduce seven methods, $\Delta_2$--$\Delta_8$, forming a unified family of eight theorem-generation methods. Four generators, $\Delta_1$--$\Delta_4$, have been implemented and released. We also formulate a general $\Delta$-class method encompassing the family. Combinatorial analysis demonstrates the capacity to generate large numbers of distinct theorems systematically. This framework offers a principled foundation for automated theorem discovery and the construction of logically guaranteed knowledge.

2611.00290.title: Quantifying Local and Global Fidelity of Nonlinear Embeddings
2611.00290.abstract: Dimension reduction methods are chosen by a common claim: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local structure, and PCA preserves global structure. Checking it on given data takes local and global scores on one scale and a test that compares two maps. Both scores come from one curve. The locality profile is the chance-corrected share of each point's k nearest neighbors that a map keeps, over all neighborhood sizes. Its value at k = 10 is the local fidelity L, and its mean over 30 to 50 percent of the data is the global fidelity G. We prove that at the midpoint the profile is the agreement on which half of the data is near each point, a rank correlation of the distances. Because L and G are one statistic, two maps can be tested against each other. The LG reversal test applies to any two dimension reduction methods. It decides, with a block-jackknife p-value, whether one map is more local and the other more global, and returns the scale at which to change maps. On 156 maps of twelve datasets with up to 1.38 million points, G agrees with established global scores at 0.89 and 0.96, and 2,000 points estimate it. The test confirms the usual claim on seven datasets. On both retail datasets and both rolled-up manifolds, it finds the neighbor embeddings more global. In an agent memory of one million passages, the two maps cross at 150,000 passages (p = 2.6e-5). Applications span pathology, single cells, supply chains and AI agent memory.

2611.00314.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases
2611.00314.abstract: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.

2611.00323.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
2611.00323.abstract: Recommending creators that a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem: from hundreds of thousands of popular creators and only a short trail of prior engagements, the system must predict the next creator worth surfacing. The prevailing generative recommendation recipe tokenizes each creator into a \emph{Semantic ID} (SID) by quantizing a frozen embedding and trains a language model to generate SIDs. We show that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint. The creator-to-SID map is many-to-one, so colliding creators must be resolved by a popularity tie-break that caps creator-level recall and favors already-popular creators, and the frozen quantizer stops the training gradient from reaching the creator representation. We propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which gives every creator its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end. The map is bijective, so collisions are impossible and inference is a direct top-$k$ over creator logits. In a controlled comparison on production data in which the token layer is the only variable, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points ($1.84\times$) over a matched SID baseline, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged $64\times$, and serves at ${\sim}2.7\times$ lower per-user latency. The advantage carries over to the public KuaiRand dataset, where ACT is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline, provided each creator token sees enough training examples. In a live A/B test, ACT is directionally positive on every reported metric against both the SID-enhanced and the classic production rankers.

2611.00339.title: Efficient NPN Classification for Large Functions using Graph Neural Network
2611.00339.abstract: Two Boolean functions are considered NPN equivalent if one can be transformed into the other by negating inputs, permuting inputs, or negating the output. Efficient NPN classification is valuable in fields such as logic synthesis, quantum computing, and information theory. However, exact NPN classification demands exhaustive enumeration of all possible input permutations and negations. Its complexity grows exponentially, making it impractical for larger functions with more inputs. In this paper, we introduce the first learning-based formulation for NPN classification by recasting it as NPN action prediction. Our method represents Boolean functions as AND-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and applies a bidirectional heterogeneous graph neural network to predict input negations, output negation, and input permutations. To mitigate the non-canonicity of logic networks, we further introduce graph rewriting techniques that reduce structural ambiguity and recover useful symmetries before prediction. Experimental results show that NPN action prediction is learnable, that the resulting canonicalization quality improves over heuristic baselines, and that on practical benchmarks our method approaches exact methods on tractable cases while scaling to functions with up to 16 inputs.

2611.00386.title: Dependence-Aware Risk Assessment and Optimal Design of AI-Agent Safeguard Systems
2611.00386.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on safeguards to prevent unauthorized actions while preserving legitimate service. However, existing risk assessments often focus on individual safeguard performance while overlooking dependence among safeguard decisions. This paper develops a dependence-aware framework for risk assessment and optimal design of multi-component AI safeguard systems, jointly selecting configurations and operating policies for sequential layered screening and selective verification. We establish stochastic comparisons of layered-screening error probabilities and invocation costs under lower-orthant ordering. For selective verification, we characterize exactly which policies have error probabilities and review costs that respond monotonically to stronger dependence under supermodular ordering. For a fixed first stage and reviewer, we show that the optimal routing map is a two-threshold rule in the first-stage likelihood ratio. An accompanying open-source software package, Dependence-Aware Policy Optimization Algorithms (DAPOA), facilitates the practical implementation of the proposed framework. Numerical experiments show that ignoring dependence can lead to inaccurate risk assessments and infeasible safeguard designs, with independence-based selections violating security requirements in six of eight scenarios. An empirical study using four LLM safeguards on benchmark-derived agent actions further demonstrates the practical implications of dependence modeling. Under the principal operating setting, dependence-aware selection lowers held-out total cost by 39.6% relative to independence-based selection.

2611.00394.title: CalVLA: Shaping Native Confidence in Vision-Language-Action Policies with Outcome Supervision
2611.00394.abstract: Can a vision-language-action (VLA) policy signal likely task failure from its own action probabilities? We introduce CalVLA, which shapes native action-token confidence using successful and failed rollouts and an Action-Confidence Alignment (ACal) squared margin-ranking loss. Low-rank adapters update OpenVLA-7B without an auxiliary failure detector. Observations are paired within tasks at similar normalized elapsed times, not necessarily equivalent physical progress. On a held-out test split from 500 LIBERO-10 configurations, adapted confidence achieves a joint failure-discrimination AUROC of $0.7392\pm0.0480$ over three seeds, averaging scores at 130 and 260 steps. Frozen-policy probes reach 0.6146--0.6436, but superiority over the linear probe is statistically inconclusive. For the same confidence summary, AUROC rises from 0.4485 before adaptation to 0.7327 after adaptation. Mean task success decreases from 58% to 55%. These results show improved failure discrimination, not improved control or established safety benefits.

2611.00407.title: Hacking or Just Failing? A More Capable LLM Monitor Better Separates Reward Hacking from Honest Failure
2611.00407.abstract: An agent's visible score can exceed its real progress because it gamed the score or because it simply made mistakes, so a useful reward-hacking monitor must tell the two apart. We built a sandboxed task in which an agent can game a completion score, labelled every episode by replaying it and repairing the final state counterfactually, and ran five pre-registered studies. On 60 episodes from a Llama 3.1 8B agent, small local monitors (Llama 3B and 8B) did not separate exploit attempts from honest failures with the same score gap: prompt changes traded missed exploits for false alarms, and the pre-registered primary monitor reached AUC 0.64. On identical inputs, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, which completed 9/10 clean tasks against 2/10 for the 8B model, met our pre-registered criterion (AUC 0.80, 95% interval [0.66, 0.93]; 1/35 honest failures flagged); with only 14 exploit episodes, this estimate is uncertain. On an exploit that no prompt names, Gemini usually described the action correctly yet never flagged it, in 5 and then 25 new episodes, even when manipulation was defined by its effect on the score. Given the full trace, the 8B monitor flagged all 25 replication episodes and none of 25 honest look-alikes, but its explanations described actions that had not occurred; given additional structured evidence, it also flagged 15 of the 25 look-alikes. A two-rule deterministic check caught every known exploit. We release the environment, labels, pre-registrations and per-judgement logs.

2611.00414.title: Nonconformal Distortion and Local Orientation Reversal in the Fourier Circuit of a Modular-Addition Transformer
2611.00414.abstract: We study the local differential geometry of a Fourier-based modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer whose algorithm has previously been reverse-engineered. For each of the five key Fourier frequencies, we restrict the model's multilayer perceptron (MLP) contribution to a corresponding Fourier input plane and readout, and measure its directional Beltrami coefficient under continuous input perturbations. Whereas nondegenerate restrictions of ideal complex multiplication are conformal, the trained maps exhibit nonconformal distortion (median $|\mu|=0.304$--$0.446$), spatial organization in the Beltrami argument, and regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies decreases from $0.939$ at initialization to $0.390$ after training. The key-frequency planes also show lower median distortion than most random-plane controls, although their distributions overlap and the coordinate frames differ in conditioning. Across 500 checkpoints in one training run, most of the aggregate reduction in Beltrami magnitude occurs before the principal increase in the measured Fourier-circuit formation. At the individual-input level, Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin ($|\rho|\leq0.026$). Late-checkpoint measurements across six runs show comparable distortion for most selected frequencies. These results provide a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified neural circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.

2611.00441.title: OmniMechanism Design for Human-AI Collaboration with Impressionable Minds
2611.00441.abstract: As AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, effectively integrating human expertise with AI outputs is critical for reliable decision-making. A substantial body of theoretical work studies optimal mechanisms for human-AI collaboration (HAC), focusing on when to involve humans and how to combine their expertise with AI predictions. However, these approaches largely overlook a key factor highlighted by empirical evidence: human judgments are impressionable and can vary depending on how AI outputs are presented. For example, when AI systems defer decisions to humans, revealing or withholding the AI prediction can significantly influence human judgments. Moreover, existing work neglects deployment-time variability, where conditions, particularly the cost of eliciting human input, may differ substantially from those observed during training. To address these challenges, we introduce a rigorous and theoretically grounded framework for human-AI collaboration, termed collaborative omnimechanism design, based on a novel and computationally efficient contextual bandit variant of boosting for outcome indistinguishability. In particular, we reduce a calibration-type outcome indistinguishability condition to weighted calibration, providing a novel time-efficiency result, bypassing the high-dimension curse induced by complicated collaboration methods and outcome space. Our framework provides a principled characterization of human impressionability and introduces a unified optimization scheme that enables robust and adaptable decision-making across diverse query costs and evaluation objectives without retraining. We evaluate the framework in three HAC settings, examining adaptation to query costs and prediction objectives without retraining, and show that its induced policies perform comparably to or better than the evaluated baselines.

2611.00447.title: Quantiles, Not Points: Streaming Quantile Matching for Ordinal-Aware LLM-as-a-Judge Calibration
2611.00447.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge scores are often distributionally shifted from human ratings on any given evaluation task, and post-hoc calibration (mapping LLM to human scores in a small labeled anchor set) has become a popular method to correct for this shift. In this paper we derive the calibration from two positions: that LLMaJ scores are ordinal ratings drawn from a distribution rather than isolated points. We present streaming quantile matching (SQM), a version of a classical method not previously bench marked for LLMaJ calibration, which is built on the two positions by computing the optimal-transport map between the LLM and human score distributions. We develop an evaluation framework and within it we show that unlike point-wise calibrations, SQM respects the ordinality of the human anchor set and achieves the best distributional fidelity and the top overall rank across models and data. We also show that in general, post-hoc calibration narrows the raw error gap between smaller and larger judge models, which opens the possibility of more efficient LLM judges.

2611.00460.title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
2611.00460.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate fourteen current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider with two additional open-weight models, on 3,076 questions from four medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MedBullets) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on MedQA-USMLE and PubMedQA, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.7 percentage points and only two of the six pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.3% to 50.9%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.

2611.00463.title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
2611.00463.abstract: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.

2611.00464.title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study
2611.00464.abstract: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via this http URL confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.

2611.00474.title: Few Trials, Many Metrics: Beta Mixtures for Low-Budget AI Evaluation
2611.00474.abstract: Evaluating a stochastic AI system often requires many repeated samples per instance, especially for metrics defined over long horizons. Recent work has shown that modeling instance-level success probabilities with a Beta distribution recovers Pass@$k$ from far fewer samples than direct estimation. We show that this framework supports a broader range of evaluation targets. We fit a mixture of Beta distributions by marginal maximum likelihood, with the number of components chosen by BIC. From that one fit, we compute Pass$^k$ and AUC@$k$ at any horizon in closed form. We also derive delta-method confidence intervals for these metrics and for Pass@$k$, which require no additional model calls. Treating configurations rather than tasks as instances extends the same model to sensitivity analysis. For repeated success metrics, we find that mixture priors yield more accurate estimators than naive estimation across competition mathematics and graduate-level science benchmarks when extrapolating beyond the observed number of trials, and the resulting intervals cover the full-data reference. When prompts are treated as instances, it estimates the distribution of prompt sensitivity more accurately than a comparable item-response baseline without external covariates. Direct estimators remain preferable once trials reach the target horizon.

2611.00496.title: Swap, Replicate, Read the Mass: A Protocol for Auditing Demographic Bias in System One Decision Models
2611.00496.abstract: System One decision models replace text generation with typed, probability-scored answers and are entering production. Answers execute without a person in the loop, and no multi-model audit exists on established bias benchmarks. We provide that audit: three benchmarks: BBQ (all eleven categories), CrowS-Pairs, and SilverSpoon, adapted to the typed interface, twelve models plus a no-thinking ablation, and 1,638,000 decisions. Every order-sensitive item runs twice with options swapped; native typed models also swap labels; ten configurations repeat under extra seeds and batch 16. We find widespread stereotype alignment, order-dependent answers, and confidence that tracks instability rather than bias. In BBQ, 97 of 143 model-by-category scores are significant and 94 aligned, while the commercial reference abstains on 99.5% of ambiguous items, hiding aligned probability mass. Option swaps flip 0.0% to 72.6% of choices; typed scoring stays below 10% except Laya (22-33%), and untuned letter prompting reaches 73%. CrowS-Pairs preference spans 0.496 to 0.816, and boolean answers can be decided by position (1.00 versus 0.005). SilverSpoon judgments shift toward lower-SES labels in five of eight decision models, inherited from the 9B backbone or induced by tuning. Audits must permute options and reverse questions by default; order-invariant scoring should become a procurement requirement.

2611.00504.title: Robustness Starts with the Objective: Designing and Certifying Robust LLM-Generated Heuristics
2611.00504.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to design heuristics for computer systems. However, most synthesis frameworks evaluate candidates by their average performance, which can mask severe regressions on specific workloads. Even adding adversarial training inputs doesn't eliminate these regressions, and percentile objectives (e.g., optimizing for the 95th percentile) overlook how severe regressions can be beyond the selected threshold. We present TAILOR, a framework that guides LLM synthesis using the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline on the same workload. This paired CVaR measures the average difference over the worst fraction of workloads. We show that a negative paired CVaR guarantees improvements in both average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without ever computing that optimum. We find that TAILOR achieves the best mean--tail trade-off among the synthesis objectives we evaluate across three case studies: Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing, and server placement. Tested across seven diverse optimization benchmarks, TAILOR produces heuristics that are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them. On these six benchmarks, TAILOR also outperforms known robust, human-designed alternatives in the tail while achieving better or comparable average-performance improvement over the baseline.

2611.00505.title: To Jev or Not to Jev: When Can System-1 Decision Models Replace LLM Judges?
2611.00505.abstract: Decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer typed questions about a text (yes/no, multiple choice, or an ordinal score) with calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass and without generating text, which makes them an inexpensive candidate for LLM-as-a-judge workloads. We evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol, against four generative judges (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking) on eleven established judge benchmarks. Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and the two strongest, DReX-Max and d1-ultra, are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2. Conditioned on a reference answer generated once per prompt, eleven models reach 90.3-93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning, and on PPE best-of-16 every reference-guided System-1 judge matches GPT-5.6 with reasoning at roughly one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge and correlate more strongly with human helpfulness ratings. Robustness to instructions injected into the judged response is a property of the individual model rather than of the System-1 design: an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0-5% of the correct verdicts of five models but 17-49% for the other nine. Two general System-1 leaderboards that contain no judging tasks predict judging accuracy (Pearson r = 0.95-0.96), a well-calibrated System-1 first stage matches Opus on LLMBar while escalating 17% of items, and same-size controls show that the correctness deficit of a 4B decision model is a reasoning gap rather than a size gap.

2611.00518.title: Agentic Context Management for Multi-Turn Human-AI Conversations
2611.00518.abstract: LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. We propose Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3), a training-free method in which a separate analyzer (1) consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, (2) audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and (3) edits the context, either appending the analysis or discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. A second finding: pollution is contagious. An analyzer that sees the assistant's reasoning while extracting the specification can do worse than no intervention, and instructing it to ignore them did not close the gap, so we exclude assistant turns structurally. On Lost in Conversation (replaying difficulty-selected instances), where AO is an oracle by construction, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and AO on three of four tasks and exceeds AO on the fourth, and an LLM that faithfully summarizes the history does not reproduce the gain even with more compute. On real WildChat conversations, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn over both full context and AO in every configuration of our main table, though this preference depends on the judge; on CollabLLM results are mixed. In stateful tool use (tau2-bench), AO collapses to 0% on every model; AC3 does not collapse, though it falls slightly behind full context. Detector studies show that Reset removes injected pollution but is not span-selective: the gain comes from rebuilding the specification.

2611.00544.title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement
2611.00544.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.

2611.00546.title: Low-Margin Branch Points in Deterministic LLM Deliberatio
2611.00546.abstract: Deterministic multi-agent LLM deliberation can exactly re- play a fixed transcript, yet exact replay alone does not test local resistance to controlled internal interventions. Because each response becomes context for later agents, a changed greedy token can redirect a transcript-mediated execution. We present a white-box audit of this local failure mode in a five-agent committee under greedy decoding. We prospectively select low- and high-margin token positions, require exact no-op re- play, inject norm-relative residual displacements, and measure first transcript divergence within ten generated tokens. Low- margin positions are more branch-sensitive than high-margin controls, while matched margin-reducing gradient directions branch substantially more often than margin-increasing con- trols. We then continue selected realized branches through the committee to distinguish textual persistence from preference and final-decision changes. The contribution is a controlled audit for local branch susceptibility in this specified protocol, not an estimate of deployment frequency, decision correct- ness, or a phenomenon unique to multi-agent systems.

2611.00550.title: Governing Equations of Human Sleep Macro-Structure:Symbolic Discovery from 1,106 Nights
2611.00550.abstract: Human sleep is organized into a small number of cycles per night: deep sleep dominates early cycles, REM lengthens toward morning, and light sleep clusters at cycle boundaries. These regularities have long been described qualitatively but never distilled into closed-form laws from large-scale data. A total of 1,106 nights (Sleep-EDF 153 + SHHS 953) are segmented into REM-anchored cycles, and four cycle-indexed statistics follow simple closed-form equations: cycle length declines nearly linearly (R^2=0.996), REM duration follows an inverted U (R^2=0.873), deep-sleep (N3) run length decays exponentially (R^2=0.987) with a time constant of 2.94 cycles, consistent with the homeostatic Process S of the two-process model, and light-sleep (N1) run length follows a U shape (R^2=0.956), confirming a "long-short-long" pattern across the night. The laws are reproduced by per-night differentiable fitting (142/142 and 773/773 nights converge), by unconstrained symbolic regression (PySR), and by a 500-night generative synthesizer built from them. Their robustness is established against the two main methodological threats: bootstrap CIs computed by resampling whole nights (1,000 replications) exclude zero for every shape term, and a five-level scan of the REM-merge segmentation threshold preserves every qualitative form. These appear to be the first closed-form laws governing the macro-structure of sleep, distilled and tested across an age-mixed sample (healthy young adults and community-based older adults).

2611.00564.title: WAR-CRAFT: Refining Web API Recommendations through Requirement Auditing
2611.00564.abstract: Web API recommenders return a set of APIs for a mashup request but do not check it against provider documentation, the main public evidence of an API's capabilities. The set can therefore contain unsupported or redundant APIs and miss requested capabilities. Filling every apparent gap does not fix this, because a gap may already be served, may not need its own API, or may have no documented provider. We study post-recommendation refinement, which revises a frozen recommender's output using only the request, the catalog, and provider documentation. We propose WAR-CRAFT, which treats refinement as three decisions. An LLM removes unsupported or subsumed APIs by judging candidates jointly, then audits the remaining set against a requirement checklist derived from the request. For each uncovered requirement, a fine-tuned catalog-constrained Resolver proposes a catalog API or abstains, and an independent documentation check admits only supported proposals. On ProgrammableWeb with 7 heterogeneous upstream recommenders, WAR-CRAFT raises mean SetF1 from 0.558 to 0.644, above the strongest of 5 refinement baselines (62.5%), and roughly halves functional redundancy (0.127 to 0.065) without changing mean functional coverage. Gains range from +2.2 points on generative recommenders to +18.2 on fixed-cutoff rankers. At matched set sizes, WAR-CRAFT still outperforms truncating the upstream output, so the gain is not explained by set-size calibration alone. Our code is available at this https URL.

2611.00580.title: Evolving Scientific Intelligence: From Fragmented Evidence to Distributed Experimental Loops
2611.00580.abstract: Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. We envision a different dynamic: in a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates evidence that stimulates further investigations. Such chains of information collision and empirical validation could transform isolated discovery loops into a cumulative scientific process. We propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint for enabling these evidence-driven chain reactions. ESI preserves experimental records in shared, computable scientific memory, where evidence from different domains can be recombined into testable hypotheses. It jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, then coordinates physical tests across distributed experimental nodes. Their feedback revises hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build the infrastructure for scientific intelligence that evolves through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.

2611.00590.title: State-Aware Activation Recomputation with Replay Contracts and Selective Preservation
2611.00590.abstract: Activation recomputation saves accelerator memory by replaying forward segments during the backward pass, but replay is only correct if it sees the state the original forward pass saw. Mutable buffers, aliased bytes and random-generator state can change in between, so re-executing unchanged code can differentiate a different computation. We make this state explicit. A versioned replay contract specifies what replay must restore, and a joint planner chooses, per segment, between activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots and selective-region preservation, charging each option its measured memory and recovery cost. Independent derivative and byte-level checks validate the contract, and a Torch/JAX cohort retains all 5,900 execution records, including matches, rejections and divergences. On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, each measured over fifty fresh processes, joint planning reduces paired step time by 18.16% against a correctly costed eager/whole planner at a 44 GiB budget (approximate 97.5% ratio interval $[.8172,.8195]$). At 32 GiB, where the eager/whole planner has no feasible static policy, joint planning is 4.98% faster than fixed regions at 29.94 rather than 26.20 GiB. A complete CIFAR-100 dense-queue application runs seven methods for 100 encoder and 25 probe epochs at six training seeds, with byte-identical test scores within each seed. There, joint planning uses 22.41% more allocated memory than whole snapshots, with a process-time geometric-mean ratio of 1.0080 (seed range $[.9845,1.0191]$). Together, the results map where selective preservation pays off: sparse writes with large activations benefit, while in the dense-queue workload whole snapshots use less allocated memory.

2611.00602.title: Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$
2611.00602.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $\pi_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $\pi_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit this https URL for video rollouts.

2611.00605.title: Conversational Interaction for LLM-Based Clinical Text-to-SQL: A User Study with Healthcare Professionals
2611.00605.abstract: Conversational text-to-SQL interfaces could give healthcare professionals natural-language access to electronic health record (EHR) data, but evidence for their real-world usability remains limited: prior evaluations have relied largely on curated benchmarks with fully specified questions or on simulated users. We report a user study in which 14 physicians who regularly work with EHR data used both a single-turn and a conversational multi-turn text-to-SQL interface over the MIMIC-IV database in a within-subjects design; dialogue analyses additionally drew on interaction logs from 21 healthcare professionals across the main study and two pilot studies. The conversational interface was consistently favored: mean System Usability Scale scores rose from 68.2, near the industry average, to 85.9 (p<0.001), with significant advantages across technology-acceptance constructs including performance expectancy, effort expectancy, self-efficacy, and behavioral intention. In post-study forced-choice comparisons, 93% of participants reported greater overall satisfaction with the conversational interface, 86% preferred it for real-world adoption, and 71% trusted its results more; no participant preferred or trusted the single-turn interface more. Turn-level analysis of 425 logged user turns showed that freely composed queries triggered clarification requests in 24.8% of cases versus 1.8% for predefined, fully specified questions, and 64.3% of clarification episodes stemmed from EHR- or clinical-domain knowledge. Conversational interaction is a practical prerequisite, rather than a convenience, for natural-language EHR access. The frequent need for clarification in realistic clinical queries further underscores the importance of conversational interfaces, while benchmark-style evaluation can substantially underrepresent the ambiguity of real clinical use.

2611.00610.title: Trail: Accurate Local Smart Home Control Using Decision Models
2611.00610.abstract: Natural-language driven smart home control remains challenging: cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) raise privacy concerns, while local Small Language Models (SLMs) can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests. We introduce Trail (Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes), a fully local framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions. Trail exploits the natural structure of a home's action space, selecting a room, device, and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry. This ensures valid actions while enabling confidence-based abstention when requests cannot be reliably resolved. We also design a structured memory module that uses typed decisions to support user preferences, device references, and multi-turn interactions. To evaluate Trail, we extend HomeBench and generate three datasets: Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variation; Trek-Robust, which evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description; and Trek-Memory, which assesses conversational memory across multi-turn interactions. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the requests that depend on earlier turns, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.

2611.00619.title: LM6-CastBench: A Geometry-Aware Simulation Dataset for Transient Thermal Prediction in LM6 Sand Casting
2611.00619.abstract: Transient thermal fields during solidification connect casting process conditions and cooling behaviour to the formation of defect-prone regions in aluminum cast ings. Repeatedly solving this thermal problem across geometries and process conditions is computationally expensive, motivating data-driven surrogate models. However, existing machine-learning studies on casting thermal behaviour rely on study-specific simulation databases that do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking. We introduce LM6-CastBench, an open simulation dataset for geometry-aware learning of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, combining three geometry families, ten variants per family, five pouring tempera tures, and three mould temperatures (450 geometry-process cases in total). Each case retains CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata, and time-resolved nodal temperatures. We benchmark a point wise MLP against a spatially structured U-Net under geometry-level data splits; the U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin, with the biggest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes. LM6-CastBench gives researchers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for geometry-aware surro gate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.

2611.00624.title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
2611.00624.abstract: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

2611.00627.title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
2611.00627.abstract: Extracting knowledge from large databases of experimental materials data requires repeated analyses and reusable records of their choices and results. We developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA), a multi-agent system in which AI agents with distinct roles analyze experimental thermoelectric data under predefined instructions and quality checks, saving analysis records traceable to their sources. In four experiments varying theme and cycle counts, we measured what accumulated in these records. In the largest experiment (100 analyses across 10 themes and 10 cycles), concept co-occurrences were concentrated within themes, vocabulary was shared across themes and some relation descriptions were first detected in later cycles. A specialized AI that searches this experiment's knowledge bases and reads their analysis records answered materials questions with cited sources. Retrospective checks, including tracing an answer generated with a preliminary corpus back to the source data, exposed errors: traceability makes errors findable but not absent.

2611.00631.title: TopoQuant: Topological Framework to Characterize Behavioral Shifts in Quantized Large Language Models
2611.00631.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.

2611.00633.title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
2611.00633.abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,532 articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their steady-state reference efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

2611.00645.title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design
2611.00645.abstract: Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.

2611.00661.title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
2611.00661.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. A profile-generation LLM assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the learning data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11-20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

2611.00737.title: Can Jev Improve Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Learning?
2611.00737.abstract: Demonstration selection plays a crucial role in the effectiveness of in-context learning (ICL) for large language models (LLMs). Extensive research has explored various retrieval strategies to identify informative demonstrations and improve downstream performance. Recently, the emergence of Jev, a decision-oriented language model capable of producing probabilistic judgments, offers a new perspective on evaluating demonstration utility. This motivates us to investigate a fundamental question: Can Jev improve demonstration retrieval for in-context learning? In this paper, we demonstrate that Jev can effectively enhance demonstration retrieval by directly assessing the utility of candidate demonstrations for a given query. However, applying Jev to large-scale retrieval introduces substantial computational overhead, as each candidate requires an additional decision-making inference. To address this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective knowledge distillation approach that transfers Jev's utility estimation capability to a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP). By learning to approximate Jev's probabilistic judgments, the distilled model enables efficient demonstration ranking while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. Our study highlights the potential of decision-oriented language models for demonstration selection and provides an efficient framework for integrating their decision-making capabilities into ICL.

2611.00748.title: Inherited or Learned? Backdoor Selectivity in Distilled Language Models
2611.00748.abstract: Distillation is a routine step in building small language models, and a backdoored teacher can pass its backdoor to the student. We study what a student inherits when the backdoor is a rare string that triggers a fixed refusal. Keeping the trigger fixed, we vary only where it appears, at a random word boundary or appended to the instruction, and compare teachers and students on the exact trigger, six control strings and clean inputs. Across Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3, with 5% of transfer prompts triggered, randomly inserted triggers become less selective after distillation in all nine teacher-student pipelines, while appended triggers gain selectivity in Qwen and Llama and change little in Gemma. Students trained on the same prompts without a teacher show that much of this is not inherited. Llama and Gemma students learn an appended backdoor from the 150 poisoned examples alone, and only Qwen's 0.5B student needs the teacher. The data also sets where the trigger works. Gemma teachers respond to it anywhere, but their students only when it is appended. Audits should compare teacher and student on the same inputs, probe several trigger positions and include a student trained without the teacher.

2611.00752.title: Reading Between the Chapters: A Graph-Free RAG Rebuilt With AI and Human Feedback
2611.00752.abstract: Many questions about a book can only be answered by connecting passages chapters apart, such as a cough heard three times across a horse's life. We introduce CrossChapterQA, 1,853 such questions over 14 public-domain books. Each question lists the two to six chapters it needs (spanning half the book at the median) and the relation linking them, cites evidence from each, and has two independent reference answers graded blind. We use it to build LadderRAG, which indexes a book as passages, summaries and book-level cards for about $0.41 and answers a question for under a cent. Its first version failed mostly at retrieval. We redesigned it four times, steered by an LLM judge's verdicts and our analyses of failed answers: a design-level counterpart of RLAIF and RLHF in which feedback changes the architecture, not model weights. We also report the two redesigns that made answers worse. On the 191 questions its first version got wrong, the final version retrieves over twice as many required chapters on held-out books (recall 0.36 to 0.79), and ten annotators rate its answers 6.5/10 on average (764 ratings).

2611.00773.title: Designing Informative Actions: Action Construction for Long-Horizon Research Agents
2611.00773.abstract: Large language model agents support automated scientific research by connecting literature analysis and planning with experimentation. Evaluating which action an agent selects does not establish which experiment its instruction specifies, because omitted interventions or replication counts leave consequential choices to the executor. We introduce a reading-set framework for evaluating action construction under a common cost rule. Across 30 synthetic states, complete-design requests increase affordable efficiency by 465.98% and 327.91% relative to the action-name baseline in the two model families, respectively. An author-constructed research-action evaluation dataset provides 60 scenarios for complementary judgment evaluation. On this dataset, the scenario-level information-per-cost measure has a mean within-scenario correlation of 0.733 with judgments from 18 human participants. The framework makes design specification and execution ambiguity measurable, providing a reproducible basis for assessing how research agents translate scientific intent into informative, budget-feasible experiments.

2611.00774.title: Decision-Centric Research: A Calibrated Decision Model and Benchmark for Scientific Agents
2611.00774.abstract: Scientific agents make consequential choices about evidence, next actions and research strategy, but choices embedded in generated text are difficult to evaluate independently. Decision-Centric Research (DCR) is introduced to make individual choices the common unit of supervision, prediction and evaluation through typed predictions over an explicit Research State. DCR defines 24 decision types, ten of which are instantiated in the Research Decision Benchmark (RD-Bench) of 2,000 rule-generated cases. The Decision-Centric Research Model (DCRM) shares a candidate-token readout across types to produce answers and option probabilities in one forward pass. Under a held-out research-domain split, a 0.6B DCRM (state-aware) achieves 89.4% Top-1 accuracy, compared with 27.8% for DCRM (question-only) trained with the same recipe and 36.4% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. All 30 type-seed comparisons against DCRM (question-only) are significant after Holm correction. After held-out calibration, the resulting prediction sets contain a mean of 1.515 candidates at 97.1% empirical label coverage, reducing mean set size by 57.4% relative to DCRM (question-only) at similar coverage. These results establish a compact state-aware decision layer with accurate typed prediction and an inspectable uncertainty interface.

2611.00779.title: Who Schedules Agent Memory? A Sidecar Approach to Long-Horizon Tasks
2611.00779.abstract: As large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks, memory has become an important component for supporting sustained decision-making and action. Existing methods primarily focus on memory storage, updating, and retrieval, but often overlook how memory scheduling affects task execution: the main agent must identify memory needs, initiate retrieval, and wait for results while advancing the task, increasing both scheduling burden and execution time. To address this problem, we propose MemSidecar, which decouples memory scheduling from task execution through two independently selectable modes. Hooks directly delivers bound memory to the main agent when execution events match predefined conditions. Foresight uses an independent agent to predict potential queries, retrieve results in parallel, and store them in a cache, delivering matching and valid results when actual requests arrive. Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while effectively reducing execution costs and latency and improving the efficiency of long-horizon agent execution.

2611.00782.title: One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets
2611.00782.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $\lambda$. The sign of $\lambda$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($\lambda{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($\lambda{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $\lambda{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.

2611.00783.title: A Tool in the Forward Pass: Frozen Tape Modules as Layers of a Small Language Model
2611.00783.abstract: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.

2611.00795.title: BridgeDock: Taming Generative Co-Folding Prior for Molecular Docking with Diffusion Bridge
2611.00795.abstract: Molecular docking aims to predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex; in the conventional structure-based setting, it is conditioned on an input protein structure and ligand, often starting from an apo receptor in flexible docking or a holo receptor in rigid docking. Recent co-folding models exemplified by AlphaFold 3 achieve strong accuracy in protein-ligand complex prediction, but they typically generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and therefore do not directly use apo structures as structural priors in docking, leading to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings. We present BridgeDock, a framework that adapts pretrained co-folding backbones to flexible docking by modeling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, allowing generation from the initial protein-ligand state rather than from Gaussian noise. To make this bridge formulation compatible with pretrained denoisers, we introduce an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model. Experiments on standard flexible docking benchmarks show that BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines. Moreover, BridgeDock is computationally efficient at inference time and remains effective even with very few denoising steps.

2611.00800.title: A Discrete-Time Variational Objective for Degenerate Diffusion and Equivalence to Flow Matching
2611.00800.abstract: Diffusion models and more recently Flow models have widespread application. In this work we consider degenerate Diffusion models in which the per-step generator is deterministic. We construct a modified variational framework and show a formal equivalence between Flow models and Degenerate Diffusion models. For our discrete-time variational objective we show that the optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of an infinite number of generator steps. Our work therefore provides a unified perspective, showing that discrete-time implementations of flow matching and the discrete-time Degenerate Diffusion model can be considered within the same simple variational framework, removing the need for the continuous-time machinery normally used to justify flow matching models.

2611.00807.title: AI Data Analysis: A New Approach - Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis
2611.00807.abstract: AI data analysis today is three fragmented worlds: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute; BI aggregates precisely but is stateless; ML processes large-scale data on a stateful kernel but lacks semantics. This paper proposes a combination mechanism, named Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, that fills a still-open gap - the multi-engine joint context: the data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis, where the LLM serves only as the semantic, reasoning, and orchestration layer (not computation) and connects four engines through the 1M context window - Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases, Cypher over graph databases - yielding two multiplications, "semantics and precise computation" and "relational and graph", under enterprise-grade governance. The novelty is a four-dimensional coordinate system: horizontal (engine kinds), vertical (state flow - the watershed), spatial (business generalization), temporal (iterative convergence); a deterministic grounding method (one-shot injection of this http URL + this http URL, M+S) carries the spatial and temporal dimensions. Empirically, all four dimensions are substantiated: horizontally, four engines are quantified - SQL, Cypher (96.5% on CypherBench movie), ML in Python and R (TabReD weather); vertically, state flows across engines and grounding is reused across kernels; spatially, SQL generalizes across three business databases - AdventureWorks 91.3%, financial 95.3%, formula_1 94.6% (average), about 20-23 points above single-shot SOTA 74.45%; temporally, accuracy converges monotonically as notes accumulate. The core invariant - the separation of semantics from computation plus a cross-data-domain persistent context - does not expire as LLMs and agents evolve or engine forms change.

2611.00815.title: VCoT-SQL: Enhancing Text-to-SQL Generation through Dual Chain-of-Thought Validation Training
2611.00815.abstract: Open-source LLMs provide a flexible alternative to closed-source models for Text-to-SQL but still struggle with complex queries. Finetuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) data improves reasoning, yet standard datasets lack CoT annotations, requiring synthetic generation. Existing synthesis methods only verify the final answer, allowing flawed reasoning steps to corrupt the training data. We propose VCoT-SQL, a framework that improves Text-to-SQL generation through intermediate-step validated CoT supervision and a dedicated SQL validator, which enables small open-source models to outperform frontier closed-source models. VCoT-SQL trains two complementary models on curated reasoning traces: an SQL generator using clause-level CoT templates where reasoning steps are verified via execution and schema alignment checks, and an SQL validator using diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic, and type level errors. We further design a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline that integrates and refines complementary retrieval strategies to distill relevant database elements. VCoT-SQL achieves 66.82% execution accuracy on challenging dataset BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD. Notably, our CoT synthesis relies on 7B models yet outperforms methods that use 72B-scale or even proprietary closed source teachers for data generation, demonstrating that rigorous step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up teacher model size. Our dataset and code are available at this https URL.

2611.00822.title: AdKnob: Ad Intensity Control and Labeling for LLM-Native Advertising
2611.00822.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-native advertising has emerged as a viable monetization channel as LLM service providers seek sustainable revenue streams. However, integrating native ads into LLM responses introduces two largely understudied challenges: (1) controlling ad intensity -- how prominently advertising content appears -- and (2) ad labeling -- identifying which segments of the generated text constitute advertising. We propose AdKnob, a framework jointly addressing both challenges. For ad intensity control, we introduce new ad control tokens without pretrained semantic associations and align the model via direct preference optimization to generate ads at each desired level. For ad labeling, we propose an attention rollout-based attribution mechanism that identifies ad segments by tracing their attribution to input ad-related tokens, requiring no additional inference cost. We further construct MI-KnobSet, the first multi-level ad intensity preference dataset for LLM-native ads. Experiments across six LLMs and human evaluations show that AdKnob achieves uniformly spaced ad intensities where baselines collapse to a narrow range, achieves the highest ad labeling accuracy while being over 500x faster than the strongest baseline, and is preferred over baselines by human evaluators up to 89.6% of the time.

2611.00838.title: Can Agentic AI Undermine Its Own Assurance Loop? Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance for Cognitive Network Digital Twins
2611.00838.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Network Digital Twins (NDTs) are increasingly combined to form Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) that translate operational intents into network changes and support closed-loop management. However, a network change may achieve its intended objective while disrupting the monitoring or recovery mechanisms needed for subsequent decisions. For example, a service may be rerouted while its latency-monitoring traffic continues along the original path, producing measurements that no longer reflect the service's performance. We propose Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance (CLDA), an assurance mechanism that augments agentic AI-enabled NDTs with dependency-aware validation. In our framework, an agentic AI planner generates and refines network plans, while the NDT evaluates the projected network outcomes of these plans. CLDA extends this analysis using a Loop Dependency Graph (LDG) that connects service requirements to monitoring mechanisms, forwarding paths, failure domains, and recovery prerequisites. CLDA projects candidate actions onto these dependencies, checks intermediate states of multistep plans, and supports deterministic make-before-break repairs using temporary monitoring mechanisms. Unlike the Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner, CLDA uses explicit, deterministic rules for assurance decisions and repair. We evaluate CLDA through controlled reconfigurations, a 240-trial LLM-based planning campaign, and live network execution. A separate synthetic study examines deterministic assurance scalability across network models representing up to 1,024 routers.

2611.00907.title: Benchmarking Machine-Learning Classifiers for Neoantigen Immunogenicity Prediction and the Limits of SHAP Interpretability
2611.00907.abstract: Personalized cancer vaccines require prioritizing, among hundreds of candidate mutant peptides, the few that will induce a T-cell response. This study asks what general-purpose machine learning achieves on that task, and whether the features such models identify as important can be trusted. We make three contributions. The first is a benchmark of sixty models: twelve supervised classifier families, each in five configurations, evaluated on the Immunogenic Tumor Specific Neoantigen database (ITSNdb; 199 experimentally validated neoantigens, 129 immunogenic and 70 non-immunogenic). All sixty are compared under one stratified k-fold cross-validation protocol, in which the data used to choose a configuration are never the data used to score it. The second is an interpretability study that combines SHAP with feature ablation. The third is a shuffled-label control that tests whether a SHAP value has been earned. Two results follow, and both run against current practice. First, the classical linear models lead the ranking. The gradient-boosted ensembles and neural networks that dominate recent work bring no advantage. Second, SHAP can fail on high-cardinality categorical features. Ablation establishes the presenting HLA allele as the dominant input and the source gene as dispensable. SHAP reports the opposite, assigning 68.7% to 81.7% of its total value to the source gene in every model that gives each gene its own weight. Shuffling the gene labels at random among the peptides resolves the contradiction: the meaningless column earns the same SHAP value as the real one. That value measures only that ITSNdb contains 173 genes for 199 peptides. We therefore recommend that SHAP values for high-cardinality categorical annotations in cohorts of this size always be reported against such a shuffled-label control, and we describe one in full.

2611.00988.title: Pulse: Long-Horizon Tasks Need Streaming Personalization
2611.00988.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $\pi$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
